chain.name: Regulated transmission and distribution utility rate base
chain.mechanism: Utilities place new transmission, substation, and distribution assets into rate base, earning an allowed return on the incremental capital.
chain.logic: The effect is levered because rate base additions compound under a regulated return while load growth from data centers provides a durable demand justification. Even a small increase in allowed capex translates directly into higher earnings from the allowed return on equity applied to the larger asset base.
chain.falsifier: State commissions cap or disallow the data center-related capex in rate cases, preventing the assets from entering rate base.

chain.name: High-voltage transformer, switchgear, and circuit breaker suppliers
chain.mechanism: Utility procurement orders for power transformers, breakers, and switchgear push supplier backlogs to multi-year levels, allowing pricing to firm.
chain.logic: Demand is levered to the scenario because long-lead grid equipment is a hard constraint: each new substation and transmission line requires multiple large power transformers and breakers, and supplier capacity is already tight. The resulting order book can exceed two years of production, shifting pricing power to manufacturers.
chain.falsifier: Utilities cancel or reschedule orders because data center load does not sign or regulators deny the underlying projects.

chain.name: Transmission and substation engineering and construction contractors
chain.mechanism: Utilities award engineering, procurement, and construction contracts for new transmission lines, substations, and grid interconnections, expanding contractor backlog.
chain.logic: The labor and specialized equipment required for transmission construction is scarce, so a given dollar of incremental capex translates into a larger share of project value captured by EPC firms through fixed-price and cost-plus contracts. Multi-year project timelines also provide revenue visibility beyond the initial order.
chain.falsifier: Utilities self-perform more work or split projects into smaller packages that reduce individual contractor backlog.

chain.name: Non-data-center commercial and industrial electricity customers
chain.mechanism: Incremental grid capex is allocated through transmission and distribution rates, raising the per-MWh delivered cost for existing customers who do not add data center load.
chain.logic: Regulators often allow utilities to recover capex through usage-based charges, so an increase in rate base without proportionate load growth from all customers raises rates for incumbents. The effect concentrates on energy-intensive industries whose margins are directly tied to electricity cost.
chain.falsifier: Regulators assign data center-specific tariffs or direct assignment of costs to the new load, insulating existing customers from the increase.

chain.name: Data center developers awaiting grid interconnection
chain.mechanism: A surge of data center interconnection requests exceeds regional grid study and upgrade capacity, delaying energization timelines and increasing deposit and network upgrade costs.
chain.logic: Interconnection queues already have multi-year study cycles, and the incremental load from data centers pushes queue volumes further beyond the available engineering and construction resources. The delay acts as a tax on data center development because schedule slippage extends time to revenue and raises the non-recurring network upgrade fees.
chain.falsifier: FERC or grid operators adopt cluster study reforms or fast-track data center requests, clearing queue bottlenecks.

chain.name: Utility rate case and prudence review exposure
chain.mechanism: Regulators respond to the capex increase by tightening prudence reviews and cost recovery conditions, which can reduce allowed returns or defer recovery of project costs.
chain.logic: As rate base requests rise, utilities face more aggressive intervention from ratepayer advocates and state commissions seeking to disallow speculative or over-budget projects. The effect is not linear because a single disallowance or cap can offset the earnings contribution from many approved projects.
chain.falsifier: Commissions accept the data center load forecasts and pre-approve the projects, leaving little room for later disallowance.

chain.name: High-voltage equipment manufacturing capacity and pricing
chain.mechanism: Equipment suppliers respond to multi-year backlog by adding factory capacity and raising prices on new orders, increasing revenue and gross margin per unit.
chain.logic: Because lead times for power transformers and breakers are already long, suppliers hold pricing power and can commit to capacity expansion only against visible multi-year contracts. The scenario converts a cyclical order spike into a longer pricing cycle as utilities accept higher prices to hold delivery slots.
chain.falsifier: A wave of imports or new competitor capacity arrives before utilities place firm orders, causing suppliers to compete on price instead.

chain.name: Behind-the-meter solar, storage, and energy efficiency providers
chain.mechanism: Rising utility rates push commercial and industrial customers to contract for on-site solar, battery storage, and demand response, adding new customer-funded projects.
chain.logic: When delivered electricity rates cross the levelized cost of distributed generation plus storage, the payback for behind-the-meter investment shortens, pulling forward discretionary energy projects. The effect is concentrated among customers with large flat load profiles and high demand charges.
chain.falsifier: Utility rates do not rise enough to make behind-the-meter economics compelling, or customers remain locked into long-term utility supply contracts.

chain.name: On-site and dedicated gas generation for data centers
chain.mechanism: Data center operators facing multi-year grid interconnection delays contract for on-site gas turbines, reciprocating engines, and fuel cells, creating a direct equipment and service revenue stream.
chain.logic: The response is driven by the opportunity cost of delay: data center revenue per MW is high enough to justify premium on-site generation even if grid power later becomes available. This creates a parallel demand channel for gas generation suppliers that is not dependent on utility procurement.
chain.falsifier: Grid operators and utilities accelerate interconnection or data center developers accept longer timelines rather than pay for on-site generation.

chain.name: High-voltage equipment suppliers face late-cycle overcapacity
chain.mechanism: Supplier capacity additions and import responses eventually outpace remaining utility demand, causing lead times to shorten and prices to fall from peak.
chain.logic: The scenario pulls forward a large amount of equipment demand, and suppliers who expand capacity based on peak order rates can overshoot when the initial wave is installed. The resulting competitive pricing erodes the gross margin gains that attracted the capacity in the first place.
chain.falsifier: Demand remains strong beyond 2030 because data center load is understated or additional grid replacement demand absorbs the new capacity.

chain.name: Regulated utility revenue erosion from customer self-supply
chain.mechanism: As C&I customers self-supply a growing share of power, utility billed volume growth weakens and the fixed cost of the expanded grid is spread over fewer remaining kWh, raising rates further for remaining customers.
chain.logic: The dynamic is self-reinforcing: each cohort of customers defecting to distributed generation raises rates for those left, which makes the next cohort's economics more attractive. Utilities with high capex relative to delivered volume face the sharpest decline in throughput.
chain.falsifier: Data center load growth offsets defection and utilities retain C&I customers through special tariffs or load retention programs.

chain.name: Gas turbine and engine service and aftermarket providers
chain.mechanism: The installed base of on-site data center gas generation creates long-term service, parts, and overhaul revenue tied to operating hours and maintenance schedules.
chain.logic: Because data center operators run on-site generation as primary or peaking power, engines accumulate run hours faster than standby units, pulling maintenance intervals forward. The aftermarket is higher margin and more recurring than the original equipment sale.
chain.falsifier: Data centers switch to grid power as soon as interconnection arrives, leaving on-site units as rarely used backup with minimal aftermarket.

quotes.text: ( Soluna or the Company ) (NASDAQ: SLNH), a developer of green data centers for intensive computing applications, including AI and Bitcoin mining, today announced it has closed the purchase of 397 acres in Briscoe County, Texas.
The Briscoe Wind Farm s Substation sits directly across from the acquired property, positioning Dorothy 3 for direct, behind-the-meter access to generation the Company owns outright.

Soluna s pioneering data centers are strategically co-located with wind, solar, or hydroelectric power plants to support high-performance computing applications, including Bitcoin Mining, Generative AI, and other compute-intensive applications.
We develop, own, and operate digital infrastructure for energy-intensive computing applications by colocating data centers with renewable energy power plants.
By locating our data centers near renewable generation assets, we seek to convert underutilized energy into economically productive computing capacity.
We utilize two distinct data center designs to serve different computing markets.
For our Bitcoin mining and hosting business, we deploy a modular data center design optimized for flexible, large-scale digital asset operations.

For AI and HPC workloads, we are developing an AI-ready data center design intended to support higher-density compute environments and customer requirements associated with advanced computing infrastructure.

Our data centers operate on a behind-the-meter basis, enabling them to draw electricity directly from the co-located renewable power plant and from the grid through the plant s existing interconnection and substation infrastructure.
In certain markets, our facilities also participate in demand response programs that support grid reliability.
A key element of our strategy is the colocation of data centers directly with renewable generation assets.

By building behind the meter at renewable generation sites, we are able to access both on-site generation and existing grid interconnection infrastructure, which we believe can improve power economics and accelerate development timelines.

6 Table of Contents We operate across multiple business lines and currently or plan to generate revenue from four primary sources: Bitcoin Mining Business We mine Bitcoin through proprietary operations and joint ventures at our data centers.
Bitcoin Hosting Business We provide hosting and colocation services to third-party Bitcoin mining customers at our modular data centers.

HPC Business Through Soluna HPC, Inc., we are developing AI-ready data center leasing and hosting capabilities for AI and HPC workloads, beginning with Project Kati 2, which is being engineered for more than 300 MW of capacity in partnership with Metrobloks, LLC ("Metrobloks").
Demand Response Business We leverage our data center infrastructure to provide demand response services to grid operators and utilities.

In 2025, our execution strategy was centered around four key initiatives: Project Optimization Enhancing the profitability, operating efficiency, and customer mix of our operating data centers, while improving customer satisfaction.

We operate data centers using both proprietary and third-party hardware and software.

High Performance Computing Business Our HPC business is being developed through Soluna HPC, Inc. and is focused on data center leasing and hosting solutions for AI and other HPC workloads, with an initial target customer base of Hyperscalers and Neoclouds, and enterprise customers over time.

# DUOT: Data center power demand creates a second revenue channel through mobile gas turbine fleet management.

## Bear case first
Why this name fails. A disconfirming reading is that the gas turbine work is an asset-management relationship, not a product sale with a visible backlog; the filing does not quantify fleet revenue or margins [4]. Insider open-market activity is zero over the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Customer evidence is thin: named counterparties are contract entities, and federal award dollars are $2.56M from one DOT contract (USASpending). The company has about 0.6 quarters of cash runway and a shelf on file, so dilution is a near-term risk (Reality check).

## Business today
The company designs, develops, deploys, and operates intelligent technology solutions, including edge data centers and power and energy consulting [0]. It sells hosting, colocation, and managed infrastructure services through edge data centers [7] and infrastructure-related services for data center deployments [14]. For the year ended 2025-12-31, revenue was $27.0M; cash at that date was $1.9M (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
DUOT occupies the on-site gas generation beneficiary node of the data center power adoption chain. The filing states the company has engaged with third parties for consulting and asset management for power solutions for large data centers supporting AI hyperscalers [3]. The economic logic is that data center operators facing grid interconnection delays may accept a premium for on-site generation; DUOT manages a mobile gas turbine fleet under contract [4].

## Customer graph
Fortress, New APR, and Sawgrass are named enterprise counterparties (Customer graph); Fortress paid a $5.0M cash advance recognized as revenue in 2025 [17]. The 10-Q refers to the fleet asset counterparty as New APR in one note [17] and Sawgrass in another [18] without explaining the relationship. The only government buyer is the Department of Transportation at $2.56M (USASpending). One other filer names the company (Customer graph). Customer evidence is thin; end-customer payments for the gas turbine fleet are not disclosed.

## Insider and management signal
No insider open-market buying or selling appeared in the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management formed a subsidiary for infrastructure services [5] and signed the Fortress fleet contract [17], but the filing does not state quantified targets or committed capex. The signal is neutral: specific operations, no insider stake change.

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is absent: analyst count, consensus, and mean target are all unavailable (Street view). Thin coverage is part of the setup for an under-covered small cap, but it also means no external validation of the thesis.

## Non-linear case
If the Fortress fleet management contract expands from consulting and operations into a large managed fleet, revenue could scale beyond the current $27.0M base (SEC XBRL). The filing describes demand for power solutions for large data centers and AI hyperscalers [3] and DUOT provides management, sales, and operations for mobile gas turbines [4]. For that outcome, data center interconnection delays must persist, Fortress must deploy additional capital, and DUOT must convert this contract into a recurring asset-management business. The current filing evidence does not show that conversion.

## Evidence
- [0] The Company designs, develops, deploys, and operates intelligent technology solutions, including edge data centers and power and energy consulting.
- [3] The Company has engaged with third parties for consulting and asset management for power solutions for large data centers supporting AI hyperscalers.
- [4] Duos Energy manages deployment and operations of a fleet of mobile gas turbines and balance-of-plant inventory under the AMA.
- [5] In 2026, the Company formed Duos Technology Solutions to provide infrastructure-related services for data center projects.
- [7] The edge data center platform is designed to generate recurring revenues through hosting, colocation, and managed infrastructure services.
- [14] Technology Solutions provides infrastructure-related services for digital infrastructure and data center deployments.
- [17] In December 2024, the Company entered contracts with Fortress to deploy and operate a fleet of mobile gas turbines; the schedule shows a $5.0M cash advance recognized as revenue in 2025.
- [18] In December 2024, the Company entered contracts with Fortress under which it will provide management, sales, and operations functions to Sawgrass in connection with the assets.

## Sizing and survivability
At $10.47M average daily dollar volume, a small fund can size a position but needs about 24 trading days to build it (Reality check). Net cash is $1.9M and cash runway is about 0.6 quarters, so the company likely needs to raise capital. Share count is up 62.1% in 12 months and a shelf is on file; dilution risk threatens the thesis (Reality check).

## What would change our mind
- A 10-K or 10-Q disclosing a named end-customer and quantified backlog for the gas turbine fleet.
- A Form 4 showing insider open-market purchases.
- A new federal award from DOE or DoD for on-site power or data center infrastructure (USASpending).
